title: Isaiah
intro: 29 days through the book of Isaiah, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Isaiah son of Amoz was a prophet in Jerusalem in the 700s BC, under four kings of Judah. His book opens like a court case, with God charging the people with injustice, and "reason together" has a legal sense, like settling a dispute. Then comes this offer of a clean slate. Starting today, 29 days through Isaiah, one verse at a time.

Isaiah's vision of the "last days": nations stream to Jerusalem to learn God's ways, God settles their disputes, and they have no more use for weapons, so they turn them into farm tools. It is one of the Bible's great pictures of lasting peace. The prophet Micah has an almost identical passage (Micah 4:1-3). A bronze sculpture inspired by this verse, a gift from the Soviet Union in 1959, stands in the garden of the United Nations headquarters in New York.

Isaiah sings a love song about a vineyard its owner tended with care, only to get sour grapes. Then he reveals that the vineyard is Israel. The ending is a Hebrew wordplay: God looked for mishpat (justice) but found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) but heard tse'aqah (a cry of distress).

In the year King Uzziah died, around 740 BC, Isaiah sees God enthroned in the temple, with seraphim, from a Hebrew word linked to "burning," calling out these words. Hebrew stresses a word by repeating it, and a threefold "holy" is rare and emphatic: God is utterly set apart, and yet his glory fills the whole earth. The song is still part of worship: Jews recite it in the Kedushah prayer, and many churches sing it as the Sanctus.

After his vision, Isaiah feels ruined, "a man of unclean lips." One of the seraphim touches his mouth with a burning coal from the altar, and his guilt is taken away. Then God asks who will go, and Isaiah answers. Christians have often read the "Us" as a hint of the Trinity, while many Jewish and modern readers see God addressing his heavenly court.

posts.display: “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.”
posts.caption: King Ahaz is panicking as two neighboring kings threaten Jerusalem, and Isaiah brings him a message from God: stay calm and trust. In Hebrew the line is a wordplay, im lo ta'aminu, ki lo te'amenu, using two forms of the root behind the word "amen," which joins the ideas of trusting and being firm.

Isaiah describes the reign of an ideal king from David's line, when even natural enemies live in peace. The popular phrase "the lion will lie down with the lamb" is a blend of this passage; Isaiah actually pairs the wolf with the lamb. The Quaker artist Edward Hicks painted this scene, which he called The Peaceable Kingdom, dozens of times.

posts.display: With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation.
posts.caption: Chapter 12 is a short song of thanks that rounds off the book's opening section. It pictures salvation, God's rescue, as fresh spring water drawn with joy, a picture of life itself in a dry land. This verse is recited in Havdalah, the ceremony that closes the Jewish Sabbath, and it became the lyrics of "Mayim Mayim," a Hebrew folk song danced in circles around the world.

This is a taunt song against the king of Babylon, mocking his fall from power: the tyrant who wanted to rise above the stars is brought down to the ground. "Day star" was a name for the morning star, the planet Venus, and the Latin Vulgate translated it as "Lucifer," meaning "light-bearer." Later Christian tradition read the passage as also describing the fall of Satan, while most scholars read it as about a human king.

Chapters 24 to 27 are often called the "Isaiah Apocalypse" because they describe the end of the age on a cosmic scale. Here God hosts a feast for all peoples and swallows up death itself. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 15, and the book of Revelation borrows the image of God wiping away every tear.

Part of a song for a restored Jerusalem. Its point is that peace comes to those whose minds rest on God in trust. In Hebrew, "perfect peace" is literally "peace, peace" (shalom shalom), a repetition that intensifies the word, and shalom means more than the absence of conflict: it carries a sense of wholeness and well-being. "Steadfast" comes from a word for leaning on something for support.

Judah's leaders were trying to make an alliance with Egypt for protection against the Assyrian empire. Isaiah urged them to rely on God instead, and they refused. The Hebrew word translated "repentance" here comes from shuv, "to turn back" or "return." Older translations render the line "in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength."

In 701 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah and sent King Hezekiah a letter mocking his trust in God. Hezekiah spreads the letter out in the temple and prays. He begins not with the danger but with who God is: the one God over every kingdom, Assyria included. Sennacherib's own account survives on clay prisms, boasting that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage," but it never claims he took the city.

Chapter 40 marks a turning point: the setting shifts from the Assyrian threat to the Babylonian exile, more than a century later, and the message turns to comfort. Here a voice contrasts fragile human life, which fades like grass, with God's word, which lasts: empires will fade, but God's promises stand. Tradition attributes the whole book to Isaiah of Jerusalem; many scholars see it as coming from more than one period, often called First, Second and Third Isaiah.

The exiles felt forgotten, complaining that their cause was ignored by God (40:27). This chapter answers by pointing to the God who made the stars and never grows tired. The Hebrew word for "wait" here, qavah, carries a sense of hopeful expectation, not just passing time. In the 1981 film Chariots of Fire, the Olympic runner Eric Liddell reads this passage aloud in a church in Paris.

This is from the first of four passages scholars call the "Servant Songs," which describe a mysterious figure God calls "My Servant." A bruised reed and a smoldering wick, an oil lamp's flame burning low, are images of the weak and nearly spent. This servant's strength shows in gentleness. Jewish interpreters have often seen the servant as Israel; Matthew's Gospel applies the passage to Jesus.

God has just told the exiles, "I have redeemed you," using the verb behind go'el, a family member who buys back a relative from debt or slavery. Passing through waters recalls Israel crossing the sea out of Egypt and crossing the Jordan into the promised land. The promise isn't that floods and fires won't come, but that they won't be faced alone.

Just before this, Isaiah mocks a woodworker who burns half a log to bake his bread, then carves the rest into a god and prays to it. Then the tone turns tender: the God who made Israel says their wrongs are wiped away like a passing cloud or a lifting mist. Many readers notice the order here: the forgiveness comes first, and the call to return follows.

Chapter 45 opens with God calling Cyrus of Persia, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let exiles go home, "His anointed" (mashiach, the word behind "Messiah"). The message to Cyrus ends with this sweeping claim that one God stands behind everything. Jewish morning prayer adapts the verse, praising God who "makes peace and creates all things," softening "calamity."

Just before this, Isaiah pictures Bel and Nebo, gods of Babylon, as idols loaded onto weary animals and hauled away in defeat. Bel was a title of Marduk, Babylon's chief god, and Nebo was his son Nabu. Israel's God reverses the picture: instead of being carried, God carries his people, from birth to old age.

Zion, a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people, complains that God has forgotten her. God answers with one of the Bible's most tender images: a mother and her nursing baby. Being inscribed on God's palms is a picture of constant remembering. Isaiah uses motherly images for God more than once, including in its final chapter.

The fourth Servant Song describes a servant who suffers for others' wrongs and is then vindicated. Christians have read it as pointing to Jesus since the New Testament (Acts 8, 1 Peter 2). Jewish tradition commonly reads the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, and Isaiah 49:3 does call the servant "Israel." "Stripes" means welts or wounds from blows.

The speakers in this song, whether the nations or Israel, admit they had misjudged the suffering servant: they were the ones who had wandered off like sheep, and he carried the cost of it. Christians see Jesus in this servant, while Jewish tradition commonly sees the people of Israel. Handel set this verse in Messiah as the chorus "All we like sheep have gone astray."

God has just invited everyone who is thirsty to come and eat and drink "without money" (55:1), and promised to "freely pardon." These lines explain why that generosity seems so surprising: God's thoughts are not human thoughts. Chapter 55 closes the section many scholars call Second Isaiah.

The people complain that they fast and God doesn't notice. God answers that the fast he wants is freeing the oppressed, pictured as breaking a yoke, the wooden bar on a working animal's neck. The next verse adds sharing bread with the hungry and sheltering the homeless. This chapter is read in synagogues on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the most solemn fast day of the Jewish year.

posts.display: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners.
posts.caption: A speaker anointed by God's Spirit announces his mission: good news for the poor, healing for the brokenhearted and freedom for captives, a message of hope to a mourning Zion. Jewish tradition and many scholars understand the speaker as the prophet himself. In Luke 4, Jesus reads this passage in the synagogue of Nazareth, then says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." "Liberty" (deror) is the word Leviticus 25 uses for the release proclaimed in the Jubilee year.

Chapter 64 is a prayer from people who feel God has hidden from them. After confessing their failures, they appeal to God as Father and as potter. Calling God "Father" is relatively rare in the Hebrew Bible, which makes it stand out here. Jeremiah 18 uses the same image of the potter and the clay.

Near the end, Isaiah's hope widens to the whole creation. The following verses picture a renewed Jerusalem where no one weeps, people live long lives, and they enjoy the houses they build and the vineyards they plant. Revelation's closing vision echoes this promise of a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

The book's last verse is grim, so when Isaiah 66 is read in synagogues, this verse is repeated after it to end on hope. Fittingly, the chapter is read when a Sabbath and a New Moon fall on the same day. The verse pictures all humanity worshiping together. That's the book of Isaiah. Thank you for reading it with me.
